summary: This informational document describes a pre-standard implementation of MPLS-TP linear protection that several operators deployed using equipment from multiple vendors. It was still carrying live traffic at publication, even though the standards-track solution is in other RFCs.

eli5.summary: Before the official rulebook was finished, some companies already played the game their own way. This RFC writes down how that early version works so people can understand it.

questions: how does pre-standard mpls-tp protection switching work
subtitle: How a pre-standard approach to fast failover in transport networks worked before the official spec arrived.

tldr.problem: Transport networks need to automatically switch traffic from a failed path to a backup path in less than 50 milliseconds, meeting strict requirements for voice and critical services.
tldr.mechanism: Linear protection switching keeps a backup path ready and switches to it when the primary path fails or degrades. The Automatic Protection Switching (APS) protocol coordinates switching between two endpoints for bidirectional paths.
tldr.outcome: This RFC documents a pre-standard implementation deployed by multiple operators before the standards-track solution in RFC 6378, RFC 7271, and RFC 7324 was finalized. These deployments were still carrying live traffic when this RFC was published.

today: RFC 7347 is Informational. It has not been obsoleted. It documents a pre-standard implementation that was deployed by multiple vendors before the IETF finished RFC 6378, RFC 7271, and RFC 7324, which are the standards-track solutions for MPLS-TP Linear Protection. The experience from deploying this pre-standard version informed the development of those standards.

sections.title: What Is Linear Protection Switching?
sections.content:
Linear protection switching is a mechanism that protects traffic paths in transport networks by automatically switching from a failed or degraded primary path to a backup path. This RFC describes a pre-standard implementation of this mechanism for MPLS-TP (MPLS Transport Profile).

The core idea is simple: a backup (protection) transport entity runs alongside the primary (working) transport entity. When the primary path fails, traffic switches to the backup immediately. The goal is to complete this switch in under 50 milliseconds to preserve services like voice calls and private lines that require minimal disruption.

This document is informational, not a standards specification. It records how several network operators deployed protection switching before the IETF standards process finished. At the time this RFC was published in 2014, these pre-standard implementations were still in operation carrying live traffic.
sections.eli5: A working path and a protection path run side by side. When the working path breaks, switches instantly kick in and reroute traffic to the protection path. This RFC explains how that switching worked in real networks before the official standard was done.

sections.title: Protection Architectures and Operating Modes
sections.content:
The RFC defines three main protection architectures. In 1+1 architecture, the source endpoint sends traffic simultaneously on both the working and protection paths. The receiving endpoint selects which one to use based on signal quality. In 1:1 architecture, traffic normally runs on the working path only. When the working path fails, both endpoints switch to send and receive on the protection path. A third type, 1:n, is mentioned as out of scope but the APS protocol is designed to support it.

Protection can be unidirectional, where each endpoint operates independently and switches only the affected direction, or bidirectional, where both directions of a path must switch together. Bidirectional switching requires the APS protocol to coordinate the two endpoints.

Two operating modes are defined. Revertive mode switches traffic back to the working path once it recovers (after a safety timer expires to avoid flip-flopping). Non-revertive mode leaves traffic on the protection path after switching, even if the working path recovers.
sections.eli5: There are two main ways to set up the backup: send on both paths and pick the better one (1+1), or send on just the main path and switch everything over if it breaks (1:1). The protection can affect one direction or both directions. You can either switch back to the main path when it heals, or stay on the backup.

sections.title: Trigger Conditions and Switching Commands
sections.content:
Protection switching is triggered by two types of conditions. Fault conditions come from Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) functions that detect problems: Signal Fail (SF) signals a hard failure, and Signal Degrade (SD) signals quality degradation. Each can affect the working or protection path.

External commands give operators manual control. Lockout of Protection (LO) disables the backup path; Manual Switch (MS) lets operators temporarily route to either path; Forced Switch (FS) moves traffic to the protection path; and Exercise (EXER) tests the APS protocol without affecting the active path. There are also local-only commands like Freeze, which stops the protection logic from responding until explicitly cleared.

These triggers are prioritized: some are higher priority than others to ensure failures always take precedence over manual commands.
sections.eli5: The system switches when it detects a broken or degraded link. Operators can also manually force switches for testing or maintenance. Some commands have higher priority so a real failure always wins over a test command.

sections.title: The Automatic Protection Switching (APS) Protocol
sections.content:
For bidirectional protection switching, the two endpoints must agree on which path to use. The Automatic Protection Switching protocol sends messages between endpoints to coordinate this. APS messages travel over the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh), an in-band channel for operations and management.

Each APS message carries request/state codes indicating which path should be active: Lockout of Protection has the highest priority, followed by Signal Fail on Protection, Forced Switch, Signal Fail on Working, Signal Degrade, Manual Switch, and No Request (the normal state). The receiving endpoint uses these codes and its own local state to decide whether to follow its own request or the far-end request.

The APS protocol also manages timers: a Hold-Off Timer delays switching to avoid thrashing when intermittent faults occur, and a Wait-to-Restore (WTR) Timer in revertive mode ensures the working path is stable before switching back.
sections.eli5: The two ends exchange messages saying "I want to use the protection path because the working path failed." They follow priority rules so both ends agree on which path to use. Timers prevent the system from constantly flipping between paths when faults come and go.

sections.title: State Transitions and Protection Logic
sections.content:
The protection switching logic is driven by a state machine. When a local condition changes (like detecting a failure) or a new APS message arrives from the far end, the logic checks both the highest local request and the far-end request. Using state transition tables defined in the RFC, it decides whether to stay in the current state or move to a new one.

For example, if the local side detects Signal Fail on the working path, it switches to the protection path and sends an SF-W message. If the far end receives that message and has no fault of its own, it acknowledges by sending NR (No Request) while using the protection path.

The RFC includes detailed state tables for all combinations: 1:1 bidirectional (revertive and non-revertive modes), 1+1 bidirectional (revertive and non-revertive modes), and 1+1 unidirectional (revertive and non-revertive modes). It also handles edge cases like simultaneous signal degradation on both paths and equal-priority requests from both endpoints.
sections.eli5: A state machine tracks what each end of the connection is doing. When the conditions change, the state machine decides what the new state should be based on priority rules. The RFC spells out all the possible state changes to prevent the two ends from disagreeing.

items.title: 1+1 Architecture
items.text: Source sends on both paths simultaneously; sink chooses the better signal.

items.title: 1:1 Architecture
items.text: Source sends on working path normally; both ends switch to protection if working path fails.

items.title: Bidirectional vs Unidirectional
items.text: Bidirectional requires APS protocol to coordinate both endpoints; unidirectional endpoints operate independently.
